'''''Kingdom of Heaven''''' is a 2005<!-- Do NOT add the film's nationality here: it is unneeded and clutters the lead --> [[historical drama]] film directed and produced by [[Ridley Scott]] and written by [[William Monahan]]. It features an ensemble cast including<!-- Billing block only; should be 7 names --> [[Edward Norton]], [[Orlando Bloom]], [[Eva Green]], [[Jeremy Irons]], [[David Thewlis]], [[Brendan Gleeson]], [[Marton Csokas]], and [[Liam Neeson]].

The film is a portrayal of the events leading to the [[Third Crusade]], focusing mainly on [[Balian of Ibelin]] who fights to defend the Crusader [[Kingdom of Jerusalem]] from the [[Ayyubid dynasty|Ayyubid]] Sultan [[Saladin]].

Filming took place in [[Ouarzazate]], [[Morocco]], and in Spain, at the [[Loarre Castle]] ([[Province of Huesca|Huesca]]), [[Segovia]], [[Ávila, Spain|Ávila]], [[Palma del Río]], and [[Seville]]'s [[Casa de Pilatos]] and [[Alcázar of Seville|Alcázar]]. The film was released on 6 May 2005 by [[20th Century Fox]] and received mixed reviews upon theatrical release. A [[director's cut]] was released on 23 December 2005 and received a more positive feedback. It grossed $218 million worldwide.

== Plot ==
In [[France in the Middle Ages|Medieval France]], Crusaders visit the village of [[Balian of Ibelin|Balian]], a blacksmith haunted by his wife's recent suicide after a miscarriage. Their leader introduces himself as Balian's father, Baron [[Barisan of Ibelin|Godfrey]], and asks him to return with him to the [[Holy Land]], but Balian declines. Later that night, Balian kills his half-brother, the greedy and immoral town priest, after discovering that he desecrated his wife's remains and stole her crucifix, while torching his smithy in the process. He joins his father's men, hoping to gain salvation for himself and his wife in [[Jerusalem]]. They are soon confronted by soldiers led by Godfrey's nephew sent to arrest Balian, during which many are killed on both sides, and an arrow strikes Godfrey. Reaching [[Messina]], they have a contentious encounter with [[Guy de Lusignan]], a prospective future king of Jerusalem who intends to break the fragile treaty between the [[Crusader states]] and [[Ayyubid Sultanate|Sultan]] [[Saladin]] with help from the brutal anti-Muslim [[Templar Knights]]. Before his death, Godfrey knights Balian and names him the new Baron so that he may obtain a military commission in Jerusalem.

Balian sails for the Holy Land, but his ship runs aground in a storm, leaving him the lone survivor. Balian journeys through the desert, recovers a horse which survived the shipwreck, and fights a Muslim cavalier over the horse. Balian slays the cavalier but spares his slave, who guides him to Jerusalem. Arriving in the city, Balian frees the slave, who tells him his mercy will earn the respect of the [[Saracens]]. Balian meets Jerusalem's leaders: the leper [[King of Jerusalem|King]] [[Baldwin IV of Jerusalem|Baldwin IV]]; [[Raymond III of Tripoli|Tiberias]], the Marshal of Jerusalem, who informs him that Saladin has forgiven the death of the cavalier; and the King's sister [[Sibylla, Queen of Jerusalem|Princess Sibylla]], Guy's wife and mother to a [[Baldwin V of Jerusalem|boy]] from an earlier marriage. Balian travels to his inherited estate at Ibelin and uses his knowledge in engineering to help the struggling residents irrigate the land. Sibylla visits him, and they become lovers.

Guy and his ally, the cruel [[Raynald of Châtillon]], attack many Saracen caravans, provoking Saladin to march on Raynald's castle despite Baldwin ordering several Templars put to death as punishment. Balian defends the castle and the nearby villagers at the king's request despite being outnumbered. After a [[Siege of Kerak (1183)|fierce battle]] that ends with the Crusaders defeated, Balian encounters the slave he freed, learning that he is actually Saladin's chancellor [[Imad al-Din al-Isfahani|Imad ad-Din]]. Imad ad-Din releases Balian in repayment of his earlier mercy. Saladin and Baldwin meet in [[parley]] and negotiate a truce. After punishing Raynald and Guy, a weakened Baldwin asks Balian to marry Sibylla and take control of the army, but Balian declines when he recognizes that Baldwin also expects him to have Guy executed. Sibylla tells Balian that a day may come when he might wish he had committed a small evil to accomplish a greater good, and she tearfully departs. Baldwin dies and is succeeded by Sibylla's son, while the fragile peace is maintained. Sibylla, learning to her horror that her son is developing leprosy like his late uncle, tearfully poisons him while he sleeps in her arms. Guy is chosen as the new king.

Guy declares war on the Saracens, attempts to assassinate Balian (who barely survives) and releases Raynald, who kills Saladin's sister. Despite Balian's advice to remain near Jerusalem's water sources, Guy marches to war, and the Saracens overwhelm the exhausted Crusaders in [[Battle of Hattin|the ensuing desert battle]]. Saladin captures Guy, beheads Raynald, and marches on Jerusalem. Tiberias evacuates the royal court to [[Cyprus]] while Balian remains behind to lead a defense. After a [[Siege of Jerusalem (1187)|devastating three-day siege]], Saladin parleys with Balian, who reaffirms he will destroy Jerusalem before Saladin can take it. Saladin offers safe conduct to all Christians within Jerusalem under Saracen rule, and Balian formally surrenders. The surviving Crusaders leave Jerusalem. Guy angrily challenges Balian to a duel, only to lose and be spared to live in shame. Sibylla renounces her claim as queen and returns with Balian to France.

A few years later, English knights [[Third Crusade|en route]] to the Holy Land visit the village of Balian, now the famed defender of Jerusalem. Balian refuses [[Richard I of England|the English king's]] offer to join his army, stating that he is merely a blacksmith. Later, Balian passes by his wife's grave as he rides with Sibylla towards the unknown. An epilogue notes that "nearly a thousand years later, peace in the Kingdom of Heaven still remains elusive".

== Production ==
[[File:Oliver Mark - Ridley Scott, Berlin 2005.jpg|thumb|Director Ridley Scott in 2005]]

=== Filming ===
Filming took place in [[Ouarzazate]], Morocco, where Scott had previously filmed ''[[Gladiator (2000 film)|Gladiator]]'' (2000) and ''[[Black Hawk Down (film)|Black Hawk Down]]'' (2001), and in Spain, at the [[Loarre Castle]] ([[Province of Huesca|Huesca]]), [[Segovia]], [[Ávila, Spain|Ávila]], [[Palma del Río]], and [[Seville]]'s [[Casa de Pilatos]] and [[Alcázar of Seville|Alcázar]].<ref>Cinemareview.com: [http://www.cinemareview.com/production.asp?prodid=2960 "Kingdom of Heaven – Production Notes"] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110726135348/http://www.cinemareview.com/production.asp?prodid=2960 |date=26 July 2011 }}</ref> Cinematographer [[John Mathieson (cinematographer)|John Mathieson]] created many large, sweeping landscapes,<ref name="SalonSZrev">{{cite web |author=Zacharek |first=Stephanie |date=6 May 2005 |title=Kingdom of Heaven |url=https://www.salon.com/2005/05/06/kingdom_2/ |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200905050941/https://www.salon.com/2005/05/06/kingdom_2/ |archive-date=5 September 2020 |access-date=19 May 2023 |work=[[Salon.com]] |quote=Cinematographer John Mathieson gives us lots of great, sweeping landscapes.}}</ref> and a large set of ancient Jerusalem was constructed based on the production design of Arthur Max.<ref name="ebert">{{cite web |author=Ebert |first=Roger |author-link=Roger Ebert |date=5 May 2005 |title=Kingdom of Heaven (review) |url=https://www.rogerebert.com/reviews/kingdom-of-heaven-2005 |work=[[RogerEbert.com]] |quote=What's more interesting is Ridley Scott's visual style, assisted by John Mathieson's cinematography and the production design of Arthur Max. A vast set of ancient Jerusalem was constructed to provide realistic foregrounds and locations, which were then enhanced by CGI backgrounds, additional horses and troops, and so on. |access-date=26 April 2022 |archive-date=26 April 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220426112235/https://www.rogerebert.com/reviews/kingdom-of-heaven-2005 |url-status=live }}</ref>

[[Orlando Bloom]] reportedly gained 10 kilograms for the part of Balian of Ibelin.<ref name="SalonSZrev"/>

=== Visual effects ===
British visual effects firm [[Moving Picture Company]] (MPC) completed 440 visual effects shots for the film.<ref name=MPC>{{cite web|title=Kingdom of Heaven VFX breakdown|url=http://www.moving-picture.com/reels/vfx-breakdowns/kingdom-of-heaven-vfx-breakdown|website=The Moving Picture Company|access-date=23 October 2014|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20141225165617/http://www.moving-picture.com/reels/vfx-breakdowns/kingdom-of-heaven-vfx-breakdown|archive-date=25 December 2014|url-status=dead}}</ref> Additionally, [[Double Negative (VFX)|Double Negative]] and [[Framestore CFC]] also contributed to complete the CGI work on the film.<ref name=dneg>{{cite web|title=Kingdom of Heaven|url=http://www.dneg.com/dneg_vfx/kingdom-of-heaven/|website=www.dneg.com|publisher=Double Negative VFX|access-date=23 October 2014|archive-date=14 October 2014|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20141014063416/http://www.dneg.com/dneg_vfx/kingdom-of-heaven/|url-status=live}}</ref>

=== Music ===
{{Main|Kingdom of Heaven (soundtrack)}}
The music differs in style and content from the soundtrack of Scott's earlier 2000 film ''[[Gladiator (2000 film)|Gladiator]]''<ref name=filmtracks>{{cite web|url=http://www.filmtracks.com/titles/kingdom_heaven.html|title=Filmtracks: Kingdom of Heaven (Harry Gregson-Williams)|website=www.filmtracks.com|access-date=25 February 2010|archive-date=2 October 2010|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20101002104911/http://www.filmtracks.com/titles/kingdom_heaven.html|url-status=live}}</ref> and many other subsequent films depicting historical events.<ref name=soundtracks>{{cite web|url=http://www.soundtrack.net/albums/database/?id=3743|title=Kingdom of Heaven Soundtrack (2005)|website=www.soundtrack.net|access-date=25 February 2010|archive-date=31 December 2010|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20101231064108/http://www.soundtrack.net/albums/database/?id=3743|url-status=live}}</ref> A combination of medieval, Middle Eastern, contemporary classical, and popular influences,<ref name=filmtracks/><ref name=soundtracks/> the soundtrack is predominantly the work of British film-score composer [[Harry Gregson-Williams]]. [[Jerry Goldsmith]]'s "Valhalla" theme from ''[[The 13th Warrior]]'' and "Vide Cor Meum" (originally used by Scott in ''[[Hannibal (2001 film)|Hannibal]]'' and composed by [[Patrick Cassidy (composer)|Patrick Cassidy]] and [[Hans Zimmer]]), sung by [[Danielle de Niese]] and Bruno Lazzaretti, were used as replacements for original music by Gregson-Williams.

== Reception ==
{{Anchor|Release|Reception}}
=== Box office ===
The film was a box office disappointment in the US and Canada, earning $47.4 million against a budget of around $130 million, but did better in Europe and the rest of the world, earning $164.3 million, with the worldwide box office earnings totalling $211,643,158.<ref>{{cite web | title = Kingdom of Heaven – Box Office Data | url = http://www.the-numbers.com/movies/2005/KINGH.php | work = [[The Numbers (website)|The Numbers]] | access-date = 9 February 2007 | archive-date = 11 June 2011 | archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20110611123443/http://www.the-numbers.com/movies/2005/KINGH.php | url-status = live }}</ref> It was also a success in [[Arabic]]-speaking countries, especially [[Egypt]]. Scott insinuated that the US failure of the film resulted from poor advertising, which presented the film as an adventure with a love story rather than an examination of religious conflict.<ref>{{cite web | title=Kingdom of Heaven Trivia| work =  Hicelebs.com| url = http://www.hicelebs.com/movies/kingdom_of_heaven/trivia.html | archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20080113030215/http://www.hicelebs.com/movies/kingdom_of_heaven/trivia.html | archive-date=13 January 2008}}</ref> It has also been noted that the film was altered from its original version to be shorter and follow a simpler plot line. This "less sophisticated" version is what hit theatres, although Scott and some of his crew felt it was watered down, explaining that by editing, "You've gone in there and taken little bits from everything".<ref>{{cite web |first=Garth |last=Franklin |title=Interview: Ridley Scott's ''Kingdom of Heaven'' |url=http://www.darkhorizons.com/news05/kingdom2.php |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20050505120239/http://www.darkhorizons.com/news05/kingdom2.php |url-status=dead |archive-date=5 May 2005 |work=[[DarkHorizons]] }}<!-- not available at https://web.archive.org/ --></ref>

=== Critical response ===
Review aggregation website [[Rotten Tomatoes]] reported that 39% of 190 critics gave the film a positive review. The site's critical consensus reads: "Although it's an objective and handsomely presented take on the Crusades, ''Kingdom of Heaven'' lacks depth."<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.rottentomatoes.com/m/kingdom_of_heaven/|title=Kingdom of Heaven|website=Rotten Tomatoes|access-date=2 June 2025|archive-date=13 February 2014|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140213233808/http://www.rottentomatoes.com/m/kingdom_of_heaven/|url-status=live}}</ref> [[Metacritic]] assigned the film a weighted averages score of 63 out of 100 based on 40 critics, indicating "generally favorable" reviews.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.metacritic.com/movie/kingdom-of-heaven|title=Kingdom of Heaven|via=www.metacritic.com|access-date=6 August 2021|archive-date=27 October 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20211027203811/https://www.metacritic.com/movie/kingdom-of-heaven|url-status=live}}</ref> Audiences polled by [[CinemaScore]] gave the film an average grade of "B–" on an A+ to F scale.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.cinemascore.com/|title=Home|website=Cinemascore}}</ref>

[[Roger Ebert]] called the film "spectacular" and found its message to be deeper than that of Scott's ''[[Gladiator (2000 film)|Gladiator]]''.<ref name="ebert"/> Stephanie Zacharek of ''[[Salon.com]]'' praised the cinematography but found the storytelling "muddled and oppressive", the battles "one long gray smudge of action with some talking in between."<ref name=SalonSZrev/> [[James Berardinelli]] wrote, "You may not leave the theater feeling better educated about history or enlightened about the Crusades, but you will leave satisfied that the filmmakers have delivered 145 minutes of exciting, visceral cinema."<ref>{{cite web |author=James Berardinelli |url=http://preview.reelviews.net/movies/k/kingdom_heaven.html |title=Kingdom of Heaven: A Film Review by James Berardinelli |website=reelviews.net |date=2005 |access-date=10 July 2017 |archive-date=24 February 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210224055156/https://preview.reelviews.net/movies/k/kingdom_heaven.html |url-status=live }}</ref> [[Geoffrey O'Brien]] describes, "The film's underlying antiheroic pessimism fits oddly with a style that aspires to the heroic."<ref>{{Cite journal |last=O'Brien |first=Geoffrey |date=2005 |editor-last=Scott |editor-first=Ridley |title=Kingdom of Heaven |url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/43457937 |journal=Film Comment |volume=41 |issue=3 |pages=71–72 |jstor=43457937 |issn=0015-119X}}</ref> John Aberth said, "''Kingdom of Heaven'' wants it far too simple to accommodate its unnecessarily convoluted plot innovations."<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Aberth |first=John |date=October 2005 |title=Kingdom of Heaven |url=https://doi.org/10.1086/ahr.110.4.1235 |journal=The American Historical Review |volume=110 |issue=4 |pages=1235–1236 |doi=10.1086/ahr.110.4.1235 |issn=0002-8762|url-access=subscription }}</ref>

Most of the cast was praised. Jack Moore described [[Edward Norton]]'s performance as the leper-King Baldwin as "phenomenal", and "so far removed from anything that he has ever done that we see the true complexities of his talent".<ref>Jack Moore, [http://www.themovieinsider.com/reviews/rid/615/Kingdom_of_Heaven ''Kingdom of Heaven: Director's Cut DVD Review''] {{webarchive |url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080622181549/http://www.themovieinsider.com/reviews/rid/615/Kingdom_of_Heaven |date=22 June 2008 }}</ref> The Syrian actor [[Ghassan Massoud]] was praised for his portrayal of Saladin, described in ''[[The New York Times]]'' as "cool as a tall glass of water".<ref>Manohla Dargis, ''The New York Times'' review of ''Kingdom of Heaven''</ref> Zacharek thought [[Eva Green]]'s [[Sibylla, Queen of Jerusalem|Princess Sibylla]] had "a measure of cool that defies her surroundings", and commended [[David Thewlis]] and [[Jeremy Irons]].<ref name=SalonSZrev/>

Lead actor Bloom's performance generally elicited a lukewarm reception from American critics, with the ''[[Boston Globe]]'' stating Bloom was "not ''actively'' bad as Balian of Ibelin" but "seems like a man holding the fort for a genuine star who never arrives".<ref>Ty Burr, "Kingdom of Heaven Movie Review: Historically and heroically challenged 'Kingdom' fails to conquer"</ref> Other critics conceded that Balian was more of a "brave and principled thinker-warrior" than a strong commander,<ref name=SalonSZrev/> and that he used brains rather than brawn to gain an advantage in battle.<ref name="CNN.com">{{cite web | date = 9 May 2005 | title = CNN "Kingdom of Heaven" Transcript | url = https://transcripts.cnn.com/ | work = CNN.com | access-date = 9 February 2007 | archive-date = 15 October 2012 | archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20121015212511/http://edition.cnn.com/TRANSCRIPTS/0505/09/i_ins.01.html | url-status = live }}</ref>

During production, Ridley Scott consulted [[Hamid Dabashi]].<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.christianitytoday.com/movies/interviews/KOHhistorians.html|title=Interviews: Kingdom of Heaven Scholars|publisher=[[Christianity Today]]|access-date=25 February 2008|archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20080219211329/http://www.christianitytoday.com/movies/interviews/KOHhistorians.html |archive-date = 19 February 2008}}</ref> Scott stated that Dabashi had approved and verified the film: "I showed the film to one very important Muslim in [[New York City|New York]], a lecturer from Columbia, and he said it was the best portrayal of [[Saladin]] he's ever seen".<ref>{{cite news|url=https://news.bbc.co.uk/2/hi/entertainment/4492625.stm|title=Film-maker defends Crusades epic|publisher=BBC News|access-date=25 February 2008|date=28 April 2005}}</ref> Dabashi praised the film for "linking historical events with contemporary issues" and called it a "work of art by a major filmmaker".<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.christianitytoday.com/movies/interviews/KOHhistorians.html|title=Interviews: Kingdom of Heaven Scholars|publisher=[[Christianity Today]]|access-date=25 February 2008|archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20080219211329/http://www.christianitytoday.com/movies/interviews/KOHhistorians.html |archive-date = 19 February 2008}}</ref>

== Academic critique and historical accuracy ==
In the time since the film's release, scholars have offered analysis and criticism within the context of contemporary international events and religious conflict, including: broad [[post-9/11]] politics, [[neocolonialism]], [[Orientalism]], the Western perspective of the film, and the detrimental handling of differences between [[Christianity and Islam]].<ref name=Schlimm>{{cite journal|last1=Schlimm|first1=Matthew Richard|title=The Necessity of Permanent Criticism: A Postcolonial Critique of Ridley Scott's Kingdom of Heaven|journal=Journal of Media and Religion|date=20 August 2010|volume=9|issue=3|pages=129–145|doi=10.1080/15348423.2010.500967|s2cid=143124492}}</ref>

Academic criticism has focused both on the directors' stylistic and artistic choices and on the depiction of a supposedly peaceful relationship between Christians and Muslims in Jerusalem and other cities.

The historical Sibylla was devoted to Guy, but the filmmakers wanted the character to be "stronger and wiser".<ref name="Smith">{{cite book |last=Smith |first=J. Lewis |title=Kingdom of Heaven: The Ridley Scott Film and the History Behind the Story |publisher=Newmarket Press |year=2005 |isbn=1557047081 |editor-last=Landau |editor-first=Diana |pages=51}}</ref> Some have said that the character of Sibylla was reimagined to fit the [[Racial fetishism|trope of exotic Middle Eastern woman]]. In contrast, historically, Sibylla and Baldwin belonged to a distinct [[Western world|Western]] class that sought to set themselves apart from Middle Eastern culture.<ref name="Neufeld">* {{cite book |last=Toswell |first=M.J. |title=The Year's Work in Medievalism, 2008 |publisher=Wipf and Stock Publishers |year=2009 |isbn=978-1725244504 |pages=89–90 |contribution=Unmasking the Leper King: The Spectral Jew in Kingdom of Heaven |contributor-last=Neufeld |contributor-first=Christine}}</ref><ref name="Francaviglia" /> While Baldwin is described in contemporary accounts as a young man vigorous in spite of his leprosy, author Christine Neufeld argued that his film depiction showed him as passive, [[androgynous]], and bound to his chamber, with there moreover being no accounts of him wearing a mask to conceal his illness.<ref name="Neufeld"/>

[[Jonathan Riley-Smith]], quoted by ''[[The Daily Telegraph]]'', described the film as "dangerous to [[Arab]] relations", calling the film "[[Osama bin Laden]]'s version of history", which would "fuel the [[Islamic fundamentalism|Islamic fundamentalists]]".<ref>{{cite news | author=Charlotte Edwardes | title=Ridley Scott's new Crusades film 'panders to Osama bin Laden' | url=https://www.telegraph.co.uk/news/worldnews/northamerica/usa/1452000/Ridley-Scotts-new-Crusades-film-panders-to-Osama-bin-Laden.html | work=[[The Daily Telegraph]] | date=18 January 2004 | access-date=2026-09-13}}</ref>

John Harlow of ''[[The Times]]'' wrote that Christianity is portrayed in an unfavourable light and the value of Christian belief is diminished, especially in the portrayal of [[Patriarch Heraclius of Jerusalem]].<ref>{{Cite news |last=Harlow |first=John |date=24 April 2005 |title=Christian right goes to war with Ridley's crusaders |language=en |work=[[The Times]] |url=https://www.thetimes.com/world/us-world/article/christian-right-goes-to-war-with-ridleys-crusaders-68h0t9lmzrq |access-date=5 March 2022 |issn=0140-0460 |archive-date=5 March 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220305040537/https://www.thetimes.co.uk/article/christian-right-goes-to-war-with-ridleys-crusaders-68h0t9lmzrq |url-status=live }}</ref>

[[Thomas F. Madden]], Director of [[Saint Louis University (United States)|Saint Louis University]]'s Center for Medieval and Renaissance Studies, criticised the film's presentation of the Crusades:

{{blockquote|Given events in the modern world it is lamentable that there is so large a gulf between what professional historians know about the Crusades and what the general population believes. This movie only widens that gulf. The shame of it is that dozens of distinguished historians across the globe would have been only too happy to help Scott and Monahan get it right.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.nationalreview.com/2005/05/onward-pc-soldiers-thomas-f-madden/ |title=Thomas F. Madden on ''Kingdom of Heaven'' on National Review Online |publisher=Nationalreview.com |date=27 May 2005 |access-date=12 March 2020 |archive-date=2 August 2020 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200802221717/https://www.nationalreview.com/2005/05/onward-pc-soldiers-thomas-f-madden/ |url-status=live }}</ref>}}

[[Medieval studies|Medievalist]] [[Paul Halsall]] defended Ridley Scott, claiming that "historians can't criticize filmmakers for having to make the decisions they have to make ... [Scott is] not writing a history textbook".<ref name="CNN.com" />

Scott said: "Story books are what we base our movies on, and what we base our characters on."<ref name="Francaviglia">{{cite book|title=Lights, Camera, History: Portraying the Past in Film|first=Richard V.|last=Francaviglia|editor-first=Jerry|editor-last=Rodnitzky|year=2007|pages=79|publisher=Texas A&M University Press|isbn=978-1585445806}}</ref> The story of Balian of Ibelin was heavily fictionalised; the historical Balian was not a French artisan but a prominent lord in the [[Kingdom of Jerusalem]]. The characters of Godfrey of Ibelin and the Hospitaller were wholly invented, while the stories of others were "tweaked"; for example, [[Raynald of Châtillon]]'s responsibility for the Christian defeat is downplayed to make Guy "more of an autonomous villain".<ref name="Smith" />

The "Director's Cut" of the film is a four-disc set, two of which are dedicated to a feature-length documentary called ''The Path to Redemption''. This contains an additional featurette on historical accuracy called "Creative Accuracy: The Scholars Speak", in which Dr Nancy Caciola said that despite the various inaccuracies and fictionalised/dramatised details, she considered the film a "responsible depiction of the period". Caciola agreed with the fictionalisation of characters because "crafting a character who is someone the audience can identify with" is necessary for a film. She said, "I, as a professional, have spent much time with [[medieval]] people, so to speak, in the texts that I read; and quite honestly there are very few of them that if I met in the flesh I feel that I would be very fond of."<ref>{{Cite video |title=Creative Accuracy: The Scholars Speak |medium=Kingdom of Heaven: Director's Cut, DVD featurette |publisher=[[20th Century Fox]] |year=2006}}</ref>

Screenwriter [[William Monahan]], who is a long-term enthusiast of the period, has said, "If it isn't in, it doesn't mean we didn't know it ... What you use, in drama, is what plays. [[Shakespeare]] did the same."<ref>{{cite news |title=Hollywood on Crusade: With His Historical Epic, Ridley Scott Hurtles Into Vexing, Volatile Territory |author=Bob Thompson |date=1 May 2005 |newspaper=Washington Post |url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/wp-dyn/content/article/2005/04/29/AR2005042900744.html |access-date=8 January 2007 |archive-date=8 April 2012 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120408005130/http://www.washingtonpost.com/wp-dyn/content/article/2005/04/29/AR2005042900744.html |url-status=live }}</ref>

Professor Dawn Marie Hayes states, "Many students felt that ''Kingdom of Heaven'' was enjoyable on a cinematic level, but cautioned against being deceived by its historical values, highlighting the perception of deliberate misleading in historical representation."<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Hayes |first=Dawn Marie |date=2007 |title=Harnessing the Potential in Historiography and Popular Culture When Teaching the Crusades |url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/30036829 |journal=The History Teacher |volume=40 |issue=3 |pages=349–361 |jstor=30036829 |issn=0018-2745}}</ref> Murray Dahm says, "''Kingdom of Heaven'' was an examination of the politics and issues of a contemporary, post-September 11, Middle East dressed up in medieval garb."<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Dahm |first=Murray |date=2016 |title=Kingdom of Heaven: A MODERN FILM IN MEDIEVAL GARB |url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/48578615 |journal=Medieval Warfare |volume=6 |issue=5 |pages=54–55 |jstor=48578615 |issn=2211-5129}}</ref>

== Extended director's cut ==
Unhappy with the theatrical version of ''Kingdom of Heaven'' (which he blamed on paying too much attention to the opinions of preview audiences, and acceding to Fox's request to shorten the film by 45 minutes), Ridley Scott supervised a [[director's cut]] of the film, which was released on 23 December 2005 at the Laemmle Fairfax Theatre in Los Angeles, California.<ref name="KoH DVD">{{cite web|url=http://www.kingdomofheavendvd.com|title=''Kingdom of Heaven: Director's Cut'' DVD official website|access-date=17 February 2020|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080907232309/http://www.kingdomofheavendvd.com/|archive-date=7 September 2008|url-status=dead}}</ref> Unlike the mixed critical reception of the film's theatrical version, the director's cut received overwhelmingly positive reviews from film critics, including a four-star review in the British magazine ''[[Total Film]]'' and a ten out of ten from [[IGN DVD]].<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.ign.com/articles/2006/06/06/double-dip-digest-kingdom-of-heaven?page=2|title=Double Dip Digest: Kingdom of Heaven|date=6 June 2006|access-date=24 July 2017|archive-date=16 August 2017|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170816111916/http://www.ign.com/articles/2006/06/06/double-dip-digest-kingdom-of-heaven?page=2|url-status=live}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=http://preview.reelviews.net/movies/k/kingdom_heaven_directors.html|title=Review: Kingdom of Heaven: Director's Cut|website=Preview.reelviews.net|access-date=10 July 2017|archive-date=24 February 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210224191738/https://preview.reelviews.net/movies/k/kingdom_heaven_directors.html|url-status=live}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.dvdtown.com/reviews/kingdom-of-heaven/3676 |title=Review of Kingdom of Heaven (Director's Cut,4-Disc) on DVD – Page 1 of 2 |website= DVDTOWN.com |access-date=25 February 2010 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090304160558/http://www.dvdtown.com/reviews/kingdom-of-heaven/3676 |archive-date=4 March 2009 }}</ref> ''[[Empire (film magazine)|Empire]]'' magazine called the reedited film an "epic", adding, "The added 45 minutes in the director's cut are like pieces missing from a beautiful but incomplete puzzle."<ref name="Kingdom">{{cite magazine|title=Directors Cuts, the Good, the Bad, and the Unnecessary|url=http://www.empireonline.com/movies/features/special-editions-good-bad-unnecessary/|magazine=Empire|date=10 January 2015}}</ref> One reviewer suggested it is the most substantial director's cut of all time<ref name="Reviewers">{{cite web |url=http://www.ugo.com/channels/dvd/features/tristanandisolde/kingdomdvdreview.asp |title=Kingdom of Heaven: 4-Disc Director's Cut DVD Review |publisher=Ugo.com |access-date=21 August 2009 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090810181722/http://www.ugo.com/channels/dvd/features/tristanandisolde/kingdomdvdreview.asp |archive-date=10 August 2009 }}</ref> and James Berardinelli wrote that it offers a much greater insight into the story and the motivations of individual characters.<ref>{{cite web|author=Berardinelli, James|url=http://preview.reelviews.net/movies/k/kingdom_heaven_directors.html|title=Kingdom of Heaven Director's Cut Review|access-date=10 July 2017|archive-date=24 February 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210224191738/https://preview.reelviews.net/movies/k/kingdom_heaven_directors.html|url-status=live}}</ref> In 2005, Scott said, "This is the one that should have gone out".<ref name="Kingdom"/>

The DVD of the extended director's cut was released on 23 May 2006. It comprises a four-disc box set with a runtime of 194 minutes. It is shown as a [[roadshow theatrical release|roadshow presentation]] with an overture and intermission in the vein of traditional Hollywood epic films.<ref name="KoH DVD"/> The first [[Blu-ray]] release omitted the roadshow elements, running at 189 minutes, but they were restored for the 2014 'Ultimate Edition' release.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.blu-ray.com/movies/Kingdom-of-Heaven-Blu-ray/110546/#Review |title=Kingdom of Heaven Blu-ray Review |author=Kauffman, Jeffrey |website=Blu-ray.com |date=5 October 2014 |access-date=17 January 2015 |archive-date=12 January 2015 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150112083608/http://www.blu-ray.com/movies/Kingdom-of-Heaven-Blu-ray/110546/#Review |url-status=live }}</ref> A remastered version was released on [[Ultra HD Blu-ray]] on May 27, 2025.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Archer |first=John |title='Kingdom Of Heaven' 4K Blu-Ray Details Announced—Including Restored And Remastered Director's Cut |url=https://www.forbes.com/sites/johnarcher/2025/04/10/kingdom-of-heaven-4k-blu-ray-details-announced-including-restored-and-remastered-directors-cut/ |access-date=25 May 2025|website=Forbes }}</ref> This version was also shown in theaters throughout the United States, as a one-night-only event, on May 14, 2025.<ref>{{cite web |last=Hunt |first=Bill |title=Breaking on the Bits-Kingdom of Heaven: Director's Cut (2005) is Coming to 4K Ultra HD on 5/27 from 20th Century Studios via Disney/Sony! |url=https://thedigitalbits.com/columns/my-two-cents/041025-0629/ |access-date=29 May 2025|website=The Digital Bits}}</ref>

Scott gave an interview to [[STV (TV channel)|STV]] on the occasion of the extended edition's UK release, when he discussed the motives and thinking behind the new version.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://video.stv.tv/bc/entertainment-hotnow-20060919-interview-ridley-scott-exclusive-/|title=Ridley Scott interview|url-status=dead|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110728054434/http://video.stv.tv/bc/entertainment-hotnow-20060919-interview-ridley-scott-exclusive-/|archive-date=28 July 2011}}</ref> Asked if he was against previewing in general in 2006, Scott stated: "It depends who's in the driving seat. If you've got a lunatic doing my job, then you need to preview. But a good director should be experienced enough to judge what he thinks is the correct version to go out into the cinema."<ref name="totalfilm">''Total Film'' magazine, July 2006: 'Three hours, eight minutes. It's beautiful.' (Interview to promote ''Kingdom of Heaven: The Director's Cut'')</ref>
